name: Cusco
scope: The Inca capital high in the Peruvian Andes (~3,400 m), whose Quechua name Qosqo means 'the navel.' T1: the Inca called their capital the NAVEL of the world -- the still point from which the empire's four quarters (Tawantinsuyu, 'the four parts together') radiated. T2: tradition holds the old core was laid out as an effigy of a sacred PUMA, with the great hilltop fortress SacsayhuamAn forming the puma's head (label as tradition/theory). T2b: SacsayhuamAn's zig-zag ramparts are built of limestone blocks, some over 100 tons, fitted so tightly without mortar that no blade slips between them. T3: the Twelve-Angled Stone on Hatun Rumiyoc street -- a single block cut with twelve corners that interlock with its neighbors -- is the emblem of Inca stonework. T3b: Inca walls survive earthquakes that topple colonial buildings on top of them, because the trapezoidal, slightly inward-leaning, mortarless blocks flex and resettle (the 1950 quake laid bare Coricancha's Inca masonry). T4: Coricancha, the Temple of the Sun, once had walls sheathed in sheets of GOLD and a garden of gold-and-silver plants. T4b: Cusco was the hub of the Qhapaq Nan, the Inca royal-road network -- roughly 40,000 km of paved highways and woven-rope suspension bridges (like Q'eswachaka) crossing the Andes, run without the wheel by relay-running chasquis. T5: the empire kept its accounts not in writing but on the QUIPU -- knotted colored cords -- administered from Cusco. Extra rung: the Inti Raymi sun festival, a June solstice celebration reborn at SacsayhuamAn.
framing_note: Place-anchored: every answer names a concrete Cusco feature (the navel, the puma layout, the twelve-angled stone, the gold-walled Coricancha, the 40,000-km road hub). Scene-led, never 'what was the Inca capital?'. Accuracy rail: the PUMA-shaped layout is a scholarly TRADITION/theory -- say so, don't state it as fact; the gold is gone because the Spanish stripped it. Dinner-test payoff: the earthquake-proof mortarless walls, or Coricancha's gold. Lane border: the Inca CONQUEST and Atahualpa's ransom belong to the history bank -- reference only as why the gold is gone; keep every rung anchored to the PLACE (stones, layout, roads, altitude).
history_overlap: The Inca rise/fall and Pizarro's conquest (1532-33) plus Atahualpa's gold ransom likely map to the history bank's Inca episode; keep these rungs anchored to the city fabric (masonry, layout, roads, altitude) and touch the conquest only as the reason Coricancha's gold vanished.

name: Lima
scope: Peru's capital on the Pacific desert coast, founded by Pizarro in 1535 as the 'City of Kings' (Ciudad de los Reyes). T1: Lima almost never rains, sitting in one of Earth's driest coastal deserts -- yet for half the year it is wrapped in a damp gray sea-fog called the garUa, which earns it the name 'the gray city' (invert: a desert city cloaked in fog that still gets almost no rain -> the garUa). T2: rising among the apartment towers of Miraflores stands Huaca Pucllana -- a great stepped PYRAMID of millions of hand-made adobe (mud) bricks raised by the pre-Inca Lima culture around 500 AD, a thousand years before the Inca. T2b: those bricks are stood on end like books on a shelf with air-gaps between them, a flexible 'bookshelf' design that has let the pyramid ride out coastal earthquakes for ~1,500 years (teach the technique). T3: the cold Humboldt Current runs right up this coast -- it chills the air, kills the rain, and feeds one of the richest fisheries on Earth just offshore (the ocean-process that makes the desert-city what it is). T4: beneath Lima's colonial cathedral and the San Francisco monastery lie CATACOMBS packed with thousands of the colonial dead.
framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name the garUa fog, the adobe pyramid, the Humboldt Current, the catacombs -- NEVER a bare 'capital of Peru.' Scene-led, never 'what is the capital of Peru?'. Accuracy rail: the huacas are adobe pyramids of the PRE-INCA Lima culture (~200-700 AD), NOT Inca -- teach that. Dinner-test payoff: a 1,500-year-old mud pyramid standing among modern apartment blocks, or a coastal city that almost never sees rain. Lane border: Peruvian food (ceviche) is the cooking bank's; the offshore fishery is an OCEAN-process fact here, not the anchovy's biology (animal bank).

name: La Paz & El Alto
scope: Bolivia's seat of government, spilling down a canyon of the high Andes at ~3,600 m -- the highest de-facto capital city in the world (Sucre is the constitutional capital). T1: to beat the traffic of a city built on canyon walls, La Paz put its commuter transit in the SKY -- Mi Teleférico, the world's longest and highest urban CABLE-CAR network, ~33 km of gondolas on ten color-coded lines gliding over the rooftops (invert: the world's longest cable-car system isn't at a ski resort -> it's the city's bus network). T2: in most cities the wealthy live high for the view; in La Paz it is FLIPPED -- the higher and colder you climb the poorer it gets, and the rich live LOWER in the warmer, more oxygen-rich Zona Sur (an altitude inversion of the usual class map). T2b: on the canyon rim sits El Alto at ~4,000-4,150 m, one of the highest big cities on Earth, with the world's highest major international airport. T3: the glacier-capped giant looming over the skyline is Illimani, ~6,438 m, the emblem of the city. T3b: just outside town, wind and rain have carved the Valle de la Luna ('Moon Valley'), a maze of clay-and-sandstone spires -- an erosion badlands (teach 'badlands'). T4: at this altitude the air holds barely two-thirds of sea-level oxygen, so newcomers get soroche (altitude sickness) -- the thin air is the single fact that shapes everything about the city.
source: Grokipedia/Mi_Teleferico (attempted, HTTP 403); corroborated en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mi_Teleferico, Guinness World Records 'largest public transit cable car network', theworld.org (PRX) 2025 report, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Paz, /wiki/El_Alto
framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name the cable-car network, the altitude inversion, Illimani, the thin air -- never a bare 'capital of Bolivia.' Accuracy rail: say 'highest DE-FACTO / administrative capital' precisely (Sucre is the constitutional capital); Mi Teleférico holds the Guinness record for largest public-transit cable-car network. Dinner-test payoff: a whole city commuting by cable car above the rooftops, or the rich-live-low inversion. Lane border: coca-leaf as a crop/food is the cooking bank's -- keep any coca rung about the ALTITUDE/thin-air place-fact.

name: Potosi
scope: A Bolivian city at ~4,000 m huddled beneath one cone-shaped mountain, Cerro Rico ('Rich Hill'). T1: in the 1600s tiny, freezing Potosí was one of the LARGEST and richest cities on Earth -- rivaling London or Paris -- because the mountain above it was riddled with SILVER (invert: a city colder and higher than almost any other was once the size of London -> the silver mountain). T2: so much silver poured out that coins minted here circulated worldwide, and the Spanish phrase 'vale un Potosí' -- 'worth a Potosí' -- came to mean 'worth a fortune.' T3: the silver was hauled out by forced laborers under the mita system, and the toll was so vast that Cerro Rico became known as 'the mountain that eats men' (death-toll estimates run into the millions but were never recorded -- label as disputed). T4: five centuries of tunneling have honeycombed Cerro Rico so completely that its summit is now SINKING and cracking -- it has lost height, a sinkhole opened near the top, and UNESCO placed the site on its 'World Heritage in Danger' list in 2014. T5: the mountain rises from the Altiplano and its silver formed in ore veins from ancient volcanic/hydrothermal fluids -- the earth-process that packed the hill (teach 'ore vein / hydrothermal').
source: Grokipedia/Cerro_Rico (attempted, HTTP 403); corroborated en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Rico, /wiki/Potosi, whc.unesco.org 'in danger' listing 2014, mongabay.com 2025 collapse report
framing_note: Place-anchored: every answer is a fact about the mountain and city (the silver, 'vale un Potosí', 'eats men', the sinking summit), never a bare date. Accuracy rail: the death toll is an unrecorded ESTIMATE -- say 'estimated/disputed', never state a number as fact. Dinner-test payoff: 'the mountain that eats men,' now caving into its own tunnels. Lane border: the silver-bankrolls-an-empire ECONOMIC/colonial story brushes the history/economics banks -- keep the anchor the MOUNTAIN and its landscape; be honest both ways about the colonial human cost.
history_overlap: Potosí silver funding the Spanish Empire and reshaping global bullion flows may belong to a history/economics episode; keep these rungs anchored to the mountain and city (silver, 'eats men', the sinking summit), not the imperial-finance narrative.

name: Rio de Janeiro
scope: Brazil's harbor city cradled between forested granite peaks and the Atlantic. T1: the name means 'River of JANUARY' -- yet there is no river; Portuguese sailors reached the great bay on 1 January 1502 and, by the traditional account, mistook its narrow mouth for a river's (label as the traditional story). T2: arms outstretched 28 m wide atop the 700 m peak of Corcovado stands Christ the Redeemer, a 30 m Art-Deco statue of soapstone completed in 1931 and later voted one of the 'New Seven Wonders of the World' (2007). T2b: the bare granite dome rising straight from the water is Sugarloaf (Pão de Açúcar), 396 m, climbed since 1912 by one of the world's first cable cars. T3: those steep bald domes are a landform -- a 'sugarloaf' or bornhardt -- ancient granite laid bare and rounded as softer rock eroded away (teach 'bornhardt/inselberg'). T3b: the deep inlet the city wraps around, Guanabara Bay, is a drowned river valley -- flooded as seas rose after the last Ice Age (a ria). T4: the green mountains INSIDE the city are the Tijuca Forest -- a hand-REPLANTED tropical rainforest; after coffee farms stripped the slopes and threatened Rio's water, workers replanted it by hand from 1861, creating one of the world's largest urban forests. T4b: samba -- the music-and-dance born in Rio's hillside neighborhoods in the early 1900s -- parades each February through a purpose-built Sambadrome at the world's biggest Carnival (a cultural creation born here). T5: the hillside favelas cling to slopes too steep to build safely, and torrential summer rain on bare granite triggers deadly landslides -- the same steep rock that makes Rio beautiful makes it dangerous.
framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name Christ/Corcovado, Sugarloaf, Guanabara, Tijuca, samba; scene-led, never 'what is Rio's famous statue?'. Accuracy rail: the 'mistook the bay for a river' naming is the TRADITIONAL account (say 'traditionally'); Christ the Redeemer completed 1931, 30 m tall. Dinner-test payoff: the hand-replanted urban rainforest (Tijuca), or 'River of January' with no river. Lane border: Brazilian food (feijoada) is the cooking bank's; samba is a cultural creation BORN here (allowed).

name: Buenos Aires
scope: Argentina's riverside capital on the Río de la Plata, the 'Paris of South America.' T1: down in the old dockside barrio of La Boca, poor European immigrants and dockworkers in the late 1800s invented a smoldering partnered dance in the tenement courtyards and cantinas -- the TANGO, Buenos Aires's gift to the world (invert: a dance now performed in ballrooms worldwide was born in a rough immigrant port district -> tango, La Boca). T2: La Boca's Caminito lane is painted in wild patchwork colors because dockworkers finished their tin-shack homes with LEFTOVER PAINT scavenged from the ships. T2b: cutting through downtown is Avenida 9 de Julio -- about 110 m across with up to seven lanes each way, recorded as the WIDEST avenue in the world, the white Obelisco standing at its heart. T3: in the Recoleta district lies a CITY OF THE DEAD -- a walled cemetery of thousands of marble mausoleums laid out like streets and plazas, where Eva 'Evita' Perón rests among Argentina's elite (a necropolis you walk like a town). T4: 'Buenos Aires' means 'good airs / fair winds,' named by Spanish sailors for a patron of favorable winds; the city sits on the flat pampas beside a river so wide (~40+ km) it looks like a muddy brown sea with no far shore.
framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name tango/La Boca, Caminito's ship-paint, the widest avenue, the Recoleta necropolis; never a bare 'capital of Argentina.' Accuracy rail: tango's origin district and era (La Boca / port arrabales, late 19th c.) stated honestly; 9 de Julio is the Guinness-recorded widest avenue (~110 m). Dinner-test payoff: Recoleta, the walk-through city of the dead (Evita's tomb), or tango born in the docks. Lane border: Argentine asado/steak is the cooking bank's; tango is a cultural creation BORN here (allowed).
history_overlap: Eva Perón / Peronism is a history-bank figure; here she is only the famous occupant of a PLACE (the Recoleta tomb) -- keep the anchor the necropolis, not her politics.

name: Valparaiso
scope: A Chilean port tumbling down some 40 steep hills (cerros) to the Pacific. T1: because the city climbs cliffs too steep for ordinary streets, since 1883 residents have ridden little wooden ELEVATOR-CARS -- the ascensores (funiculars) -- hauled up the hillsides on cables; at their peak around 30 ran, and ~16 survive as national monuments (invert: a public 'elevator' that runs outdoors up a hillside -> Valparaíso's ascensores). T2: the hills are a maze of houses painted every color and clad in corrugated metal salvaged from ships -- an accidental rainbow that made the 'Historic Quarter of the Seaport City of Valparaíso' a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003. T3: Valparaíso was once THE great Pacific stop for sailing ships rounding Cape Horn -- until the Panama Canal opened in 1914, ships stopped taking the long way, and the boomtown fell quiet (a place undone by a distant canal). T4: the poet Pablo Neruda built one of his hillside houses here, La Sebastiana, for its sweeping view over the harbor (a cultural anchor to the place).
framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name the ascensores, the painted UNESCO hills, the Cape-Horn-to-Panama-Canal turn; never a bare 'port in Chile.' Accuracy rail: first ascensor 1883, ~16 of ~30 survive; UNESCO 2003. Dinner-test payoff: the outdoor hillside 'elevators' (ascensores) that are really funiculars. Lane border: none major.

name: Ushuaia
scope: The 'End of the World' city on Tierra del Fuego, facing the Beagle Channel. T1: Ushuaia is billed as the world's SOUTHERNMOST city -- the last true city before Antarctica and the main jumping-off port for Antarctic expedition ships (a smaller Chilean town, Puerto Williams, actually lies a little further south -- state the caveat). T2: the island's name Tierra del Fuego means 'Land of FIRE' because Magellan's expedition in 1520 saw the campfires and smoke of the native Yamana people burning along the shore (label as the traditional naming-story). T3: the channel in front of the city, the Beagle Channel, is named for HMS Beagle -- the survey ship that carried Charles Darwin through these waters in 1833 (the PLACE is named for the ship, not the dog).
framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name 'southernmost city / Antarctic gateway', 'Land of Fire', 'the Beagle Channel'; scene-led. Accuracy rail: state the Puerto Williams caveat honestly (Ushuaia is the southernmost CITY; a smaller Chilean town lies further south), and the Magellan-fires naming as the traditional account. Dinner-test payoff: 'Land of Fire,' named for the natives' shore-fires. Lane border: the Beagle Channel is named for the SHIP -- Darwin's voyage is a history/science episode; keep the anchor the PLACE, never the beagle-the-animal or Darwin's biology.
history_overlap: Darwin's Beagle voyage is a history/history-of-science episode; here the channel is only a named PLACE anchored to the ship's passage.

name: Brasilia
scope: Brazil's capital -- a whole city conjured from empty savanna in the 1950s. T1: Brazil's capital had been Rio on the crowded coast; to pull the country inland the government built a brand-new capital, Brasília, on bare highland scrub -- and raised the entire city in just 41 MONTHS, inaugurating it in 1960 (invert: a national capital built from nothing in under four years). T2: seen from the air, the master plan -- the Plano Piloto by Lúcio Costa -- reads like a giant AIRPLANE or bird, its curved 'wings' lined with housing and its 'fuselage' holding the government (Costa himself called it a crossing of two axes). T2b: architect Oscar Niemeyer filled it with white curving concrete landmarks -- the crown-of-thorns glass Cathedral, the bowl-and-dome National Congress, the ministry towers -- making Brasília a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987 for its modernist design. T3: the city sits on the cerrado, Brazil's vast tropical SAVANNA, on a high plateau (~1,100 m) -- chosen as neutral central ground far from any existing coastal power. T4: to give the dry inland capital a shoreline, engineers dammed a river to create the artificial Lake Paranoá, wrapping the planned city in water (a made landscape).
framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name '41 months', the airplane-shaped plan, Niemeyer's cathedral, the cerrado plateau; never a bare 'capital of Brazil.' Accuracy rail: built in 41 months, inaugurated 1960; the 'airplane' is how the Plano Piloto reads from the air (Costa described it as two crossing axes). Dinner-test payoff: a national capital shaped like an airplane, built from scratch in under four years. Lane border: Kubitschek's politics belong to the history bank -- keep the anchor the CITY's plan and highland site.

name: Manaus
scope: A city of nearly two million in the middle of the Amazon rainforest, reachable mostly by boat or plane. T1: just below the city two great rivers meet but REFUSE TO MIX -- the coffee-black Río Negro and the sandy-tan Río Solimões run side by side in two unblended stripes for about 6 km before finally merging into the Amazon (the 'Meeting of the Waters'). T2: the reason they don't mix: the black Negro is warm (~28 C) and slow, the pale Solimões is cold (~22 C), fast, and heavy with Andean silt -- differences of temperature, speed, and sediment keep the two waters apart (the earth-science answer). T3: in the 1890s rubber made Manaus so rich its barons built a gilded European OPERA HOUSE deep in the jungle -- the Teatro Amazonas (opened 1896) -- with roof tiles from France, marble from Italy, and a dome of 36,000 tiles in Brazil's colors. T4: Manaus exists because it stands where the rainforest's rivers converge -- before roads, the Amazon and its tributaries WERE the highways, and the city was the inland port of the rubber trade. T5: the Río Negro runs black because it drains sandy lowland forest and carries dissolved plant tannins (like strong tea) with almost no sediment -- a 'blackwater' river (teach 'blackwater vs whitewater').
framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name the Meeting of the Waters, the jungle opera house, the blackwater Negro; never a bare 'city in Brazil.' Accuracy rail: ~6 km side-by-side, with the temperature/speed/sediment reason stated correctly; Teatro Amazonas opened 1896. Dinner-test payoff: a gilded European opera house in the middle of the jungle, or the two-color river that will not mix. Lane border: the rubber-boom economics is history's -- keep the anchor the PLACE (the building, the rivers); Amazon WILDLIFE (pink dolphins) is the animal bank's, so keep the water/landscape the fact.

name: Sydney
scope: Australia's harbor city on one of the world's great natural harbors, Port Jackson. T1: Sydney's most famous building looks like a cluster of white SAILS or shells rising from the water -- the Sydney Opera House, opened in 1973 (invert: 'the sails by the water' -> the Opera House). T2: for years no one could figure out how to build those swooping shells -- until architect Jørn Utzon realized every shell could be cut from the surface of ONE imaginary SPHERE, so they'd all share the same curve and could be mass-cast from common moulds (the geometry breakthrough of 1961). T2b: the shells are clad in over a MILLION tiles (about 1,056,000) made in Sweden, in two finishes -- glossy white and matte cream -- so the roof shimmers in a subtle chevron pattern and never looks flat. T3: arching over the harbor is the steel Sydney Harbour Bridge, opened in 1932 and nicknamed 'the Coathanger' -- one of the world's widest long-span steel-ARCH bridges, which daring visitors now climb to the summit of. T3b: Sydney Harbour itself is a ria -- a river valley DROWNED by rising seas after the last Ice Age -- which is why its shoreline is so long, branching, and deep enough for great ships (teach 'ria / drowned valley'). T4: the city is built on honey-colored 'Sydney sandstone' (Hawkesbury sandstone), laid down by ancient rivers ~230 million years ago, and cut into its cliffs, harborside 'Heads', and old buildings.
source: Grokipedia/Sydney_Opera_House (attempted, HTTP 403); corroborated en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Opera_House (Utzon, 1973, ~1,056,006 Hoganas tiles, sphere geometry), /wiki/Sydney_Harbour_Bridge, /wiki/Port_Jackson, /wiki/Hawkesbury_Sandstone
framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name the Opera House, the one-sphere geometry, the million tiles, the Coathanger, the drowned-valley harbor; scene-led, never 'what is Sydney's famous building?'. Accuracy rail: Opera House opened 1973 and every shell is a section of ONE sphere; Harbour Bridge opened 1932. Dinner-test payoff: every sail cut from a single sphere, or the harbor as a drowned river valley. Lane border: none major.

name: Melbourne
scope: Australia's second city, famous for hiding its best life down narrow LANEWAYS. T1: between Melbourne's grand streets runs a hidden web of skinny LANEWAYS -- once service alleys, now packed with cafes, tiny bars, and wall-to-roof STREET ART (Hosier Lane's ever-changing murals) -- the city's living rooms (invert: the city's coolest streets are its old back-alleys -> the laneways). T2: Melbourne rattles along on the LARGEST urban TRAM network in the world -- about 250 km of track, 24 routes, 500+ trams -- kept running when almost every other city tore its tramlines out. T2b: to avoid blocking those trams, drivers make a bizarre 'HOOK TURN' -- turning RIGHT from the far LEFT lane (a place-specific quirk written into the streets). T3: Melbourne was built rich and fast on the GOLD RUSH of the 1850s, when strikes at nearby Ballarat and Bendigo made Victoria one of the world's great goldfields and paid for 'Marvellous Melbourne's' grand boulevards and gardens. T4: the city sits on flat volcanic basalt plains at the head of Port Phillip Bay and is famous for 'four seasons in one day' -- cold fronts off the Southern Ocean can swing the weather wildly within hours (a place's climate quirk).
source: Grokipedia/Melbourne (attempted, HTTP 403); corroborated en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trams_in_Melbourne (largest network, ~250 km, 24 routes, 500+ trams), /wiki/Hosier_Lane, /wiki/Victorian_gold_rush
framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name the laneways/street art, the tram network, the hook turn, the gold rush; scene-led. Accuracy rail: it is the LARGEST urban tram network in the world (~250 km) -- state it as such; gold rush of the 1850s. Dinner-test payoff: the hidden street-art laneways, or the world's biggest tram network. Lane border: Melbourne coffee CULTURE is a place-culture aside -- keep any laneway rung about the PLACE, not coffee-as-a-drink (cooking bank).
history_overlap: The Victorian gold rush may be a history/economics episode; keep the rung anchored to how the gold BUILT the city (its boulevards and wealth), not the rush narrative.

name: Auckland
scope: New Zealand's biggest city -- built on top of a field of VOLCANOES. T1: Auckland is dotted with about 50 small volcanoes -- roughly 53 cones, craters, and lava hills poking up among the suburbs -- the whole city sitting on a live VOLCANIC FIELD (invert: the green cones scattered across the city are -> volcanoes). T2: the biggest and YOUNGEST, Rangitoto, is a near-perfect cone that rose straight out of the SEA only about 600 years ago -- recent enough that the Maori living nearby SAW it erupt (a volcano younger than most cathedrals). T2b: because each eruption bursts up in a NEW spot (a 'monogenetic' field), geologists warn the next Auckland volcano won't reopen an old crater -- it will break out somewhere brand new (teach 'monogenetic volcanic field'). T3: Auckland is squeezed onto a narrow ISTHMUS between two harbors -- the Waitemata on the Pacific side and the Manukau on the Tasman side -- so narrow that Maori once dragged their canoes overland between the two seas. T4: with more boats per person than almost anywhere, Auckland is the 'City of Sails,' and its Sky Tower (328 m) is the tallest freestanding structure in the Southern Hemisphere. T5: the Maori name Tamaki Makaurau -- 'Tamaki desired by many' -- reflects how the fertile volcanic soil and twin harbors made it the most fought-over ground in the land.
framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name the volcanic field, Rangitoto, the isthmus, the City of Sails; scene-led, never 'how many volcanoes...?'. Accuracy rail: ~53 volcanoes, Rangitoto ~600 years old and witnessed by Maori, a monogenetic field (each eruption a NEW vent). Dinner-test payoff: a whole city on a live volcanic field where the next eruption will pick a fresh spot, or Rangitoto rising from the sea within human memory. Lane border: none major.

name: Wellington
scope: New Zealand's capital, wedged between steep green hills and a harbor at the bottom of the North Island. T1: Wellington is reckoned the WINDIEST city in the world -- gales gust over 60 km/h on roughly 170+ days a year -- because the full force of the 'Roaring Forties' is funneled through the narrow Cook Strait straight onto the city (invert: 'Windy Welly' -> the Cook Strait wind funnel). T2: the city straddles a plate boundary: the active Wellington FAULT runs right through downtown, where the Australian and Pacific plates grind past each other. T2b: much of central Wellington stands on land the sea once covered -- the great 1855 Wairarapa earthquake LIFTED the harbor floor and created new dry ground the city later built on (an earth-process you can stand on). T3: Wellington is the world's SOUTHERNMOST capital of a sovereign country (~41 S) -- nearer to Antarctica than any other national capital. T4: those steep hills and clear harbor light made it 'Wellywood' -- Peter Jackson's Weta studios filmed and built The Lord of the Rings here, turning New Zealand's landscapes into Middle-earth (a cultural creation rooted in the place).
source: Grokipedia/Wellington (attempted, HTTP 403); corroborated blog.metservice.com 'Windy Wellington', en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellington, /wiki/Wellington_Fault, /wiki/1855_Wairarapa_earthquake
framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name the Cook Strait wind funnel, the Wellington Fault, the lifted 1855 shoreline, the southernmost capital; scene-led. Accuracy rail: back the 'windiest city' claim with real numbers (gales ~170+ days/yr); the Wellington Fault marks the Australian/Pacific plate boundary. Dinner-test payoff: downtown built on seabed heaved out of the harbor by the 1855 quake, or the windiest capital on Earth. Lane border: The Lord of the Rings is a film (cultural creation) rooted in NZ landscape -- fine as one place-culture rung.

name: Rotorua
scope: A Maori town in the middle of New Zealand's geothermal heartland, where the GROUND itself steams. T1: the whole town smells of rotten eggs -- because the earth beneath Rotorua leaks SULFUR gas (hydrogen sulphide) from the hot rock below, earning it the nickname 'Sulphur City' (invert: the rotten-egg smell -> geothermal sulfur gas). T2: in the Whakarewarewa valley, Pohutu Geyser -- the LARGEST active geyser in the Southern Hemisphere -- blasts boiling water up to 30 m into the air, around twenty times a day (a named wonder). T2b: nearby, scalding pools and plopping MUD POOLS simmer, and the Champagne Pool (Wai-O-Tapu) fizzes inside a bright orange rim of arsenic and antimony minerals (a colored hot spring; earth-chemistry). T3: at the Whakarewarewa 'living village' the local Te Arawa Maori have used the geothermal ground for centuries -- bathing in the hot pools and COOKING in the natural steam and boiling springs (a place-culture that harnesses the heat). T4: all this heat exists because Rotorua sits inside the Taupo Volcanic Zone -- a stretch of the North Island being slowly pulled apart, where magma lies close beneath a thin crust and boils the groundwater (the earth-engine; teach 'geothermal / volcanic rift').
source: Grokipedia/Pohutu_Geyser (attempted, HTTP 403); corroborated en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pohutu_Geyser (largest in S. Hemisphere, up to 30 m), aa.co.nz, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotorua, /wiki/Taupo_Volcanic_Zone, /wiki/Champagne_Pool
framing_note: Place-anchored: answers name the sulfur smell, Pohutu Geyser, the mud/Champagne pools, the living Maori village, the Taupo Volcanic Zone; scene-led. Accuracy rail: Pohutu is the largest geyser in the SOUTHERN HEMISPHERE (not the world), ~30 m; the smell is hydrogen sulphide. Dinner-test payoff: a living village that bathes and cooks in the natural steam, or the biggest geyser south of the equator. Lane border: steam-cooking (hangi) is a place-culture MENTION of the village harnessing the ground's heat -- keep the answer the geothermal PLACE-fact, not a recipe or ingredient (cooking bank); respect the living Maori village on its own terms.
